deck.headline: Nvidia board weighs ousting Jensen Huang as a second affair is reported
deck.sub: The WSJ says the board is preparing to remove its founder; shares fell about 8% after hours, and no decision had been announced by publication.
deck.summary: Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Jensen Huang after the WSJ said it was preparing to oust him and the NYT reported a second affair, with an executive who reports to him. Bloomberg says a successor search firm is involved. Shares fell about 8% after hours. No decision yet.
deck.whyItMatters: Nvidia is the largest weight in global equity indexes and the centre of AI supply. A forced exit with no succession plan hits index funds, AI-infrastructure credit and the chip-export debate in Washington at once. Watch for a board statement before the US open.
deck.update: Escalated: the WSJ reports the board is preparing to oust Huang; the NYT reports a second relationship with VP Kimberly Powell; the board met on Wednesday; shares fell ~8% after hours
deck.checked: Checked on the FT's report (via Ars Technica), Business Insider and The Japan Times; WSJ, NYT and Bloomberg seen only as headlines
deck.storyline: Storyline: who can buy top AI chips · day 11
deck.detailHtml:
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to weigh the future of Jensen Huang, its only chief executive in 33 years, the FT reports (text via Ars Technica), after the Wall Street Journal said the board was preparing to oust him. The New York Times reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice-president of healthcare, who reports to him. Bloomberg says the board is working with an outside firm to identify replacements and may name an interim CEO. Nvidia declined to comment to the NYT; on Sunday the board had backed Huang after he admitted an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a customer whom US intelligence believes was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Shares fell about 8% after hours (Business Insider); CoreWeave, Supermicro, Micron and TSMC fell 2-5%. No decision had been announced by publication.

Three reports landed within hours on Wednesday evening, US time: the WSJ said the board was preparing to remove Huang and would meet as soon as that day; the NYT, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, said he had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, an 18-year Nvidia veteran who reports to him; and Bloomberg said the board was working with an outside firm on possible successors and weighing a temporary CEO. The FT confirmed the board meeting. Nvidia has made no statement on the Powell report. On Sunday the board said it backed Huang while former US Attorney Joon Kim of Wachtell investigates whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

deck.headline: Google ships Gemini Decision 1, a model that decides instead of writing
deck.summary: Google launched Gemini Decision 1, a model that answers up to 1,000 yes/no, choice or scoring questions about one input (text, images, audio, video or PDF) in a single pass instead of writing text. It returns calibrated probabilities in 150-250 ms for $0.10 per million input tokens, with no output charge.
deck.whyItMatters: Decision models are becoming a standard building block. For banks they fit routing, policy checks, document triage and fraud flags, where a calibrated probability and a fixed latency matter more than prose. Three vendors now sell the same shape of API, so switching costs are low.
deck.checked: Checked on Google's launch post and Vercel's changelog; comparison with Jev from Simon Willison
deck.storyline: Storyline: new kinds of AI models · day 3
deck.detailHtml: Google DeepMind launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 (gemini-decision-1). Instead of writing an answer token by token, it scores the options you give it in a single forward pass and returns probabilities and confidence scores. One request can carry one input of text, images, audio, video or PDFs (up to 256K tokens) plus up to 1,000 independent questions of three kinds: yes/no, choice and rubric scores. Google quotes 150-250 ms end to end, $0.10 per million input tokens and no output charge, says it leads its benchmark suite with the lowest calibration error, and says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite on that suite. Vercel's AI Gateway listed it the same day. Simon Willison notes the API copies TypeSafe's Jev almost exactly (Google now joins Jev and OpenAI's decision model); Jev stays cheaper at 4.2 cents per million but handles only text.

deck.headline: Deutsche Bank switches on crypto custody for institutions
deck.summary: Deutsche Bank has switched on crypto custody for institutional and corporate clients in Europe. They can hold and move Bitcoin, Ether, USDC, EURC and EURAU, with the bank managing keys under its MiCA registration. It also plans tokenised money-market funds and stablecoin work with DWS.
deck.whyItMatters: Germany's largest bank now holds crypto for clients under MiCA. That makes custody a standard bank product in Europe, and puts pressure on rivals to offer it, and on crypto-native custodians on price.
deck.checked: Checked on Cointelegraph (citing the bank's announcement); the September plan on Bloomberg Law
deck.detailHtml: Deutsche Bank launched its digital-asset custody service on Wednesday for institutional and corporate clients, Cointelegraph reports from an announcement shared with it (Reuters also reported the launch). Clients can store and transfer Bitcoin, Ether and selected stablecoins (USDC, EURC and AllUnity's EURAU); the bank manages the wallets and private keys. Its entry in the EU's MiCA register for custody and transfer is dated 12 October, with BaFin as supervisor. The bank also signed a memorandum of understanding with its asset manager DWS to explore tokenised money-market funds, crypto exchange-traded commodities and stablecoins. It first announced the plan on 16 September.

deck.headline: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights for customers
deck.summary: United Airlines is banning personal AI agents such as Meta's Muse from booking or changing flights for customers, on its own sites and through travel agencies. It cites shared passwords, unintended purchases and miles use, and federal check-in rules. It is the first big merchant to block consumer agents outright.
deck.whyItMatters: The first big merchant to shut the door on consumer agents. Banks and card networks building agent payments (agent tokens, agentic checkout) now face merchants who want to decide which agents may transact, which turns agent identity and liability into a commercial negotiation.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI agents that buy things · day 4
deck.detailHtml: United Airlines said it is banning third-party personal AI agents from making reservations for travellers, CBS News reports (the NYT and The Information also covered it). United says sharing account credentials with such assistants can expose sensitive data and lead to unintended purchases, account changes or use of MileagePlus miles, and that an agent checking someone in could breach federal rules, such as travellers confirming in person that bags hold no banned items. It will restrict access on its own platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators, and is updating its booking terms. An analyst told CBS United does not want another powerful intermediary between it and its customers.

deck.headline: Fractile raises $720m to stack memory on AI inference chips
deck.summary: London's Fractile raised $720 million, valuing it at about $7 billion, with UK sovereign-fund backing. Its inference chips stack ordinary DRAM directly on each chip so large models can run long agent tasks without the usual memory-speed trade-off. It is among the best-funded challengers to Nvidia for inference.
deck.whyItMatters: Inference cost is where AI spending is heading, and memory, not maths, is the bottleneck. A credible non-Nvidia design with sovereign backing gives buyers, including banks running models in-house, another future supplier. It ships nothing in volume yet.
deck.storyline: Storyline: the race for AI chips and compute · day 12
deck.detailHtml: Fractile, a London start-up building chips for running AI models (inference), raised a $720 million Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, with backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund, TechCrunch reports. The UK government put the valuation at over £5 billion; the FT and a Reuters source say about $7 billion. The product: after a pivot, Fractile stacks ordinary DRAM directly on top of each chip to avoid the usual trade-off between memory capacity and speed, which bites when agents run long chains of tasks on big models, and it ships its own compiler to schedule models on the hardware. Sifted had first reported the £540m raise.

deck.headline: Hackers hijack ScreenConnect to reach dozens of MSP customers
deck.summary: Attackers are abusing cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect to plant their own remote-access tools: Huntress counts 6 compromised managed service providers and 286+ machines at 47 organisations, still rising. ConnectWise is investigating and tells partners to avoid live sessions with suspect devices. Firms using outsourced IT should check now.
deck.whyItMatters: Outsourced IT is a direct path into regulated firms. Banks and insurers should ask their MSPs today whether they use cloud ScreenConnect, what was run on their endpoints since 11 November, and pause interactive sessions until ConnectWise reports.
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks on IT management tools · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Security firm Huntress is tracking an active campaign, which began around 17:47 UTC on 11 November, against cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect instances used by managed service providers (MSPs), BleepingComputer reports. At last count: 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints across 47 organisations, and rising. Attackers use ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to install their own remote-access clients on customers' machines. Huntress also warns of a possible reverse pivot: compromising a technician's workstation when they open a session to an infected device; it is unclear whether that uses a vulnerability. ConnectWise confirmed it is investigating and told partners to avoid interactive remote sessions with potentially compromised devices. The same week, N-able pulled its N-central RMM offline after 33 alleged zero-days were published.

deck.headline: N-able disables N-central remote control after 33 zero-days go public
deck.summary: A researcher published 33 alleged zero-days in N-able's N-central IT management platform, with working exploit code. N-able took its hosted service offline, then shipped a hotfix for seven CVEs that switches off built-in remote control for now. On-premises customers were told to stay offline until patched.
deck.whyItMatters: Two of the main tools MSPs use to run client IT were hit in the same week. Any firm whose IT provider runs N-central on premises should confirm Hotfix 2 is installed and that agents and probes were updated.
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks on IT management tools · day 3
deck.detailHtml: Researcher Sean Bales published 'Able2Shell' on 9 November: 33 alleged zero-days with proof-of-concept code in N-able N-central, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by MSPs, including four exploit chains to code execution, two as root and one needing no credentials. N-able took hosted N-central offline as a precaution, told on-premises customers to stay offline until patched, and on 10 November shipped Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), a critical release covering seven CVEs (XXE, OGNL injection, privilege escalation, XSS, SSRF and path-traversal RCE). It disables built-in remote control until a future fix, Infosecurity reports. Hosted environments are back online.

deck.headline: CoreWeave results lift AI stocks after a week of selling
deck.summary: CoreWeave shares jumped about 10% after third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion beat forecasts and it signalled an end to heavy borrowing, lifting AI stocks and US indexes on Wednesday. The relief was brief: CoreWeave fell 4% after hours when reports said Nvidia's board might remove its CEO.
deck.whyItMatters: AI-infrastructure credit has been the market's worry (CoreWeave bonds yielded over 16% last week). Better numbers help, but the after-hours reversal shows how much the whole trade still hangs on Nvidia.
deck.storyline: Storyline: building AI's power and data centres · day 14
deck.detailHtml: CoreWeave, which rents out Nvidia-based AI computing, rose about 10% on Wednesday after third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion beat expectations and management signalled it was done piling on expensive debt, Crypto Briefing reports; the WSJ and Economic Times credit CoreWeave with lifting the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. The bounce came less than a week after a historic AI-stock selloff (WSJ). After the close, CoreWeave fell more than 4% as Nvidia slid on the board report (Business Insider). Techmeme also relays a report that CoreWeave plans an investment-grade loan of $4B+ as soon as next week (not checked).

deck.headline: SoftBank writes off $3.7bn on gas turbines it ordered for AI
deck.summary: SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion after cancelling gas turbines it had ordered to power US AI data centres, helping drive a $7 billion quarterly net loss. It is the first large loss from the rush to lock up power equipment for AI.
deck.whyItMatters: The AI power rush produced a turbine queue, and the first big over-order is now a loss. Lenders to data-centre projects should check how much of a sponsor's power plan rests on reservations that can be cancelled or resold.
deck.storyline: Storyline: building AI's power and data centres · day 15
deck.detailHtml: SoftBank Group took a ¥597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) writedown after cancelling gas-turbine orders it had placed to power AI data centres in the United States, Crypto Briefing reports; The Information and Tom's Hardware also covered it. The charge helped drive a ¥1.12 trillion ($7 billion) net loss for the fiscal second quarter. Tom's Hardware notes it came days after SoftBank denied a claim by Elon Musk about its turbine orders.

deck.headline: MSCI drops Strategy from its indexes as a bitcoin holding company
deck.summary: MSCI will drop Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, from its USA, World and ACWI indexes on 30 November after classing it as a non-operating company. Funds tracking those indexes must sell. Metaplanet and three other asset-holding companies are also being cut.
deck.whyItMatters: Index funds that track MSCI benchmarks must sell by month-end, removing a steady source of demand for the biggest bitcoin treasury company. It also sets a precedent: holding crypto as the main business now counts as not operating.
deck.storyline: Storyline: money in and out of crypto · day 3
deck.detailHtml: MSCI will remove Strategy (MSTR) from the MSCI USA Index at the close on 30 November, which also takes it out of MSCI World and ACWI, after a new screen classified it as a non-operating issuer, Bitcoin Magazine reports from MSCI's November 2026 index review; Cointelegraph confirms. Japan's Metaplanet, uranium holder Yellow Cake, Iceland's Skel and micro-cap Upexi are also deleted. All five were already flagged on MSCI's potential-impact list built on 30 September data.

deck.headline: AWS ships an emulator written entirely by AI agents, unreviewed by humans
deck.summary: AWS released AWS Emulator, a free tool that runs AWS services locally for testing. Amazon says every line was written by thousands of autonomous AI agents that write tests and fix bugs with no human code review. The code is public on GitHub under a CC0 licence.
deck.whyItMatters: A hyperscaler is shipping software no person reviewed, which pushes the question of how to trust agent-written code from theory into practice. Teams can use it to test AWS workloads offline; treat it as a test tool, not production infrastructure.
deck.detailHtml: AWS released AWS Emulator, a local emulator of AWS services that it says was 100% written by autonomous AI agents. In a post, senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg says thousands of agents write tests, find issues and fix code without human review; the source is on GitHub under a CC0 licence and is constantly updated. GeekWire, via Techmeme, says it simulates 200+ services and that the team has not written or reviewed any of the code. It drew 626 points on Hacker News.

deck.headline: DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 predicts how gene variants act cell by cell
deck.summary: Google DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2, a DNA model that predicts how genetic variants change gene activity in hundreds of specific human cell types. DeepMind says it helps find the cells that drive a disease; independent tests and access terms are still to come.
deck.whyItMatters: Most disease-linked variants sit outside genes and act in particular cell types; a model that says which cells a variant affects narrows drug-target searches. Watch for access terms and independent benchmarks before treating the claims as settled.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI doing science and maths · day 4
deck.detailHtml: Google DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2, its next DNA sequence model. Where last year's AlphaGenome predicted how DNA variants affect gene regulation, version 2 predicts how sequences and variants change gene activity in hundreds of specific human cell types, bridging single-cell maps such as the Human Cell Atlas and human genetics. DeepMind pitches it as a way to find which cells drive a disease, and published a paper alongside.

deck.headline: IBM plans a 1,040-qubit linked quantum system for 2027
deck.summary: IBM will offer a quantum system of two linked Nighthawk chips, about 1,040 qubits, in 2027, scaling back a plan to link nine chips but keeping its qubit target. It still aims for error-corrected machines before 2030. Quantinuum separately upgraded RIKEN's quantum computer and teamed up with SoftBank.
deck.whyItMatters: This is Thursday's deep beat. Bigger, linked chips are steady progress, not code-breaking: banks' post-quantum migration timelines do not change, but the 'harvest now, decrypt later' risk keeps the deadline real.
deck.detailHtml: At its Quantum Developer Conference, IBM updated its roadmap, Ars Technica reports. A new Nighthawk general-purpose processor version (r3) has over 500 programmable qubits (SiliconANGLE: 520, running 10,000 operations); IBM will link two of them (not nine, as planned) for about 1,040 qubits on offer in 2027, keeping the total qubit target. It still aims for error-corrected quantum computers before the decade is out, on a separate development track, and credits hardware-based qubit resets in September's chips for a performance jump. Separately, Quantinuum upgraded its machine at Japan's RIKEN and agreed to deploy with SoftBank in AI data centres (DCD, headline).

deck.headline: Spain's first general strike in 14 years ends in Barcelona clashes
deck.summary: Spain held its first general strike in 14 years over housing and living costs. About 120,000 marched in Madrid and over 50,000 in Barcelona, where masked groups clashed with police. Transport was disrupted. Spain votes in a general election on 29 November.
deck.whyItMatters: Housing costs are now an election-deciding issue in one of the euro area's fastest-growing economies. Spanish banks' mortgage books and any housing-tax or rent-control promises in the campaign are the things to watch.
deck.detailHtml: Spain's main unions held the country's first general strike in 14 years, over housing and the cost of living, the BBC reports. Some 120,000 people marched in Madrid and more than 50,000 in Barcelona, where masked groups burned bins, smashed windows and looted shops as police fired tear gas. Transport and public services were badly disrupted. UGT's Pepe Álvarez called turnout "massive". Spain votes in a general election on 29 November.

deck.headline: Houthi missiles over Mecca as Iran denies talks; oil bounces
deck.summary: Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and the Mecca region; debris fell near Mecca. The Houthis deny targeting the holy city and say they hit the Yanbu export hub. Brent rebounded towards $93 as Iran denied talks with the US.
deck.whyItMatters: Yesterday's dip below $90 did not last. Attacks on the routes that bypass Hormuz keep a risk premium in oil, and with it in inflation and the case for a December Fed hike.
deck.update: Escalated: Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and the Mecca region; strike on Yanbu pumping station; Brent rebounds from below $90 to ~$93
deck.storyline: Storyline: the Iran war and the economy · day 3
deck.detailHtml: Saudi Arabia's civil defence said debris from two ballistic missiles intercepted over the Mecca region fell in several places, Reuters reports (via ThePrint). Earlier the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed three cruise missiles headed for Riyadh, two drones aimed at Mecca and southern areas and two more missiles (Reuters via Cyprus Mail). The Houthis denied targeting Mecca and said they hit a pumping station at Yanbu, the Red Sea hub that lets Saudi crude avoid the blocked Strait of Hormuz. Brent jumped about 3% to ~$94 when Iran denied any talks with Washington (OilPrice), then settled below $93 (Bloomberg via Mint). Iran's top negotiator Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera Hormuz will "never return" to its pre-war status and that Iran and Oman will oversee it. Saudi output rose 26% in October.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGReuters via ThePrint · Reuters via Cyprus Mail · OilPrice · Mint (Bloomberg) · Al Jazeera

deck.headline: Notion confirms Fireworks breach exposed AI chat transcripts
deck.summary: Notion confirmed that the breach at its AI provider Fireworks exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces, taken from the data behind its admin Insights feature. Notion cut off Fireworks, deleted its data there and disabled Insights.
deck.whyItMatters: Usage-analytics features quietly keep copies of prompts. Ask SaaS vendors which sub-processors hold chat logs, for how long, and for what features.
deck.update: Notion's own disclosure: transcripts from its Insights dataset in a small number of workspaces were exposed; Insights disabled, Fireworks traffic cut
deck.storyline: Storyline: leaked and stolen AI keys and data · day 8
deck.detailHtml: Notion disclosed that the breach at its AI infrastructure provider Fireworks AI exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces, BleepingComputer reports. The transcripts came from the dataset behind Insights, a feature that shows admins how teams use AI, which Notion has now disabled. Fireworks alerted Notion on 2 November about an exposed dataset it said held only synthetic test data; Notion cut traffic to Fireworks, deleted all its data from Fireworks' systems and halted training runs by 3 November; Fireworks confirmed on 8 November that customer data had been accessed. Fireworks runs some open-weight models in Notion AI.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBleepingComputer · Insurance Journal (Bloomberg)OTHERHacker News thread (164 pts)

alsoToday.headline: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi's Senate seat
alsoToday.summary: The Associated Press called Mississippi's US Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, just over a week after the election, Rolling Stone reports; he led by about 2,000 votes the day after polling and widened the margin.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Every extra Democratic Senate seat strengthens the incoming majority that will set crypto, bank-capital and AI rules from January.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: the 2026 US midterms' aftermath · day 1
alsoToday.detailHtml: The Associated Press called Mississippi's US Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, just over a week after the election, Rolling Stone reports; he led by about 2,000 votes the day after polling and widened the margin. The Guardian notes he will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since 1874. Rolling Stone calls it the most shocking of the Democrats' midterm upsets, which included a statewide sweep in Texas.

alsoToday.headline: Bessent moved to a military base after Iran-linked threats
alsoToday.summary: Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary who leads the economic blockade of Iran, has been moved from his Washington home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, the BBC reports, citing CBS.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Iran's response to sanctions is reaching the officials and infrastructure behind them, in the US and Europe.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: the Iran war and the economy · day 3
alsoToday.detailHtml: Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary who leads the economic blockade of Iran, has been moved from his Washington home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, the BBC reports, citing CBS. A source said concern rose after a photo in the Wall Street Journal let his Georgetown home be geolocated. US intelligence has warned Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including officials. Treasury said Bessent "will not be deterred". France this week blamed Iran's Revolutionary Guards for sabotaging refrigeration controllers at about 700 shops.

alsoToday.headline: France says Iran's Guards sabotaged fridges at 700 shops
alsoToday.summary: The French government says a cyber unit of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Shahid Kaveh (known through personas such as CyberAveng3rs), broke into refrigeration controllers at about 700 retail sites on the night of 11 October and set defrost temperatures high, spoiling food and causing at least 15 fires, The Hacker News reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Internet-exposed building controls are now a state target in Europe, not just the US. Retail lenders and insurers should expect claims and questions on operational-technology security.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: hacks that hit the physical world · day 2
alsoToday.detailHtml: The French government says a cyber unit of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Shahid Kaveh (known through personas such as CyberAveng3rs), broke into refrigeration controllers at about 700 retail sites on the night of 11 October and set defrost temperatures high, spoiling food and causing at least 15 fires, The Hacker News reports. Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation into the unit's head and two deputies and requested international arrest warrants; the foreign ministry will summon Iran's ambassador and seek new EU sanctions.

alsoToday.headline: New York proposes $3m-a-day fines for frontier AI safety breaches
alsoToday.summary: A New York bill called RAISE Act 2.0 would fine frontier AI developers by the day: up to $1 million a day for a first safety violation and $3 million a day for later ones (up to $90M over 30 days), PYMNTS reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: With Democrats taking Congress, state rules like New York's are likely to set the bar that federal law then copies.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: US state AI laws · day 1
alsoToday.detailHtml: A New York bill called RAISE Act 2.0 would fine frontier AI developers by the day: up to $1 million a day for a first safety violation and $3 million a day for later ones (up to $90M over 30 days), PYMNTS reports. It would cover any developer that spent over $1 billion on its models over three years and require annual outside safety audits, quarterly reports on research run by AI, and a senior officer's certification of filings. Governor Hochul this week also launched what Politico calls the first state AI testing programme (not opened).

alsoToday.headline: Gartner: AI to create 1.7 million more jobs than it cuts by 2030
alsoToday.summary: Gartner forecasts AI will create 10.6 million jobs and remove 8.9 million by 2030, a net gain of 1.7 million, Insurance Business reports. In asset-intensive industries (the largest share of jobs) it expects 6.4M created and 6M eliminated, with losses hitting 0.4% of workers.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A forecast, not data. It is useful mainly as a counterweight to cut-heavy narratives when boards set AI headcount targets.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Gartner forecasts AI will create 10.6 million jobs and remove 8.9 million by 2030, a net gain of 1.7 million, Insurance Business reports. In asset-intensive industries (the largest share of jobs) it expects 6.4M created and 6M eliminated, with losses hitting 0.4% of workers. Nearly 70% of the technology workforce is highly exposed, yet Gartner expects the sector to add 1.9M and lose 0.4M. In Australia, CNA reports companies face 'AI washing' accusations after job cuts and offshoring.

alsoToday.headline: Cowbell launches insurance for mistakes made by AI agents
alsoToday.summary: Cowbell, a California cyber insurer for small and mid-sized firms, will launch Cowbell AI liability insurance in January 2027: a standalone policy for agentic AI that executes tasks, moves money, files documents and talks to customers without a human approving each step, Insurance Business reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A priced market for agent errors is forming. Banks offering agent payments to small businesses will want to know whether their clients' losses are insured, and by whom.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Cowbell, a California cyber insurer for small and mid-sized firms, will launch Cowbell AI liability insurance in January 2027: a standalone policy for agentic AI that executes tasks, moves money, files documents and talks to customers without a human approving each step, Insurance Business reports. Cover is triggered by a defined 'AI incident' and combines first-party losses with third-party liability. It fills a gap left as ISO's CG 40 47 endorsement lets carriers exclude generative-AI injury and damage from general liability. Separately, Insurance Business reports banks are seeking credit-insurance cover for a surge in AI-related lending.
alsoToday.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGInsurance Business · Life Insurance International

alsoToday.headline: ECB warns digital euro could slip past 2029 without a deal this year
alsoToday.summary: Piero Cipollone of the ECB's Executive Board told the European Parliament's economic committee that EU negotiators should reach a deal on the digital euro regulation by year-end, Cointelegraph reports. The ECB aims to be ready for a first issuance in 2029 if the law passes this year; "a delay in adoption could instead postpone the introduction," he said, warning of deeper dependence…
alsoToday.whyItMatters: For euro-area banks the timeline drives spending on wallets, holding limits and deposit outflow planning; a slip buys time but prolongs uncertainty.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Piero Cipollone of the ECB's Executive Board told the European Parliament's economic committee that EU negotiators should reach a deal on the digital euro regulation by year-end, Cointelegraph reports. The ECB aims to be ready for a first issuance in 2029 if the law passes this year; "a delay in adoption could instead postpone the introduction," he said, warning of deeper dependence on foreign payment providers. The Governing Council decides on issuance only after the law passes.

alsoToday.headline: India's fund inflows cool as US yields hit bonds; rupee firms
alsoToday.summary: Net inflows into Indian equity mutual funds fell 14% in October to ₹33,000 crore (~$3.5bn) from ₹38,310 crore, AMFI data show (Bloomberg via Mint), as investors grew wary of small and mid caps after the Nifty 50 hit its lowest since April 2025 early in the month; debt funds took in ₹1.13 trillion.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Domestic SIP money has been the cushion against foreign selling; if it cools while US yields rise, Indian banks' bond portfolios and treasury income feel it first.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: India's markets and money flows · day 1
alsoToday.detailHtml: Net inflows into Indian equity mutual funds fell 14% in October to ₹33,000 crore (~$3.5bn) from ₹38,310 crore, AMFI data show (Bloomberg via Mint), as investors grew wary of small and mid caps after the Nifty 50 hit its lowest since April 2025 early in the month; debt funds took in ₹1.13 trillion. On Wednesday India's 10-year bond had its worst day in a month as US Treasuries sold off after hot US inflation (Reuters via ET), while the rupee closed at 93.69 per dollar, its strongest since April, on foreign buying of Indian stocks.

alsoToday.headline: Europe's electric car sales jump 49% as China's fall
alsoToday.summary: Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide in October, up 8% year on year, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence data reported by Electrek. Europe sold 510,000 (+36%), with battery-electric cars up 49%; China fell 12% to 1.14M; North America rose 24% to 0.13M, its first year-on-year rise in 2026; the rest of the world grew 85%.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Europe and emerging markets now carry EV growth while China cools, which matters for auto-loan books and battery-metal prices.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: the shift to electric cars · day 3

alsoToday.headline: eMudhra revokes 16 CA certificates over a key-handling script bug
alsoToday.summary: eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority, revoked eight more intermediate CA certificates, bringing the total to 16, BleepingComputer reports. Its incident report says both sets were affected by a custom Python script used in April 2025 to transfer CA private keys between hardware security modules from different vendors after new hardware was delayed; a bug weakened the keys, and the first eight were…
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Certificates chained to these intermediates stop working; Indian banks and government services that use eMudhra for TLS or document signing should check their chains.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 8
alsoToday.detailHtml: eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority, revoked eight more intermediate CA certificates, bringing the total to 16, BleepingComputer reports. Its incident report says both sets were affected by a custom Python script used in April 2025 to transfer CA private keys between hardware security modules from different vendors after new hardware was delayed; a bug weakened the keys, and the first eight were so weak anyone could recover them almost instantly.

alsoToday.headline: Stablecoin supply falls $14bn in a month, most since 2022
alsoToday.summary: Total stablecoin supply has fallen about $14 billion in 30 days, the fastest decline since June 2022, Crypto Briefing reports. Bitcoin hovered near $74,000 (Cointelegraph) as ETF investors kept selling (CryptoSlate).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Stablecoins are the cash leg of crypto; a shrinking float usually means money leaving the market, which banks launching custody and tokenised products will feel in volumes.

alsoToday.headline: Tether shows a sub-billion-parameter agent that runs on the phone
alsoToday.summary: Tether AI Research, the stablecoin issuer's research arm (QVAC), published BotPsy on the Hugging Face blog: an on-device personal assistant built on a 0.8-billion-parameter agentic language model. The authors argue routine tasks do not need frontier models, that cloud models' costs and access can change without notice, and that small specialised agents can match them on narrow jobs while keeping data on…
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Small agent models running locally are the privacy-friendly route for customer-facing assistants in regulated firms; benchmark claims still need independent checks.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: new kinds of AI models · day 4
alsoToday.detailHtml: Tether AI Research, the stablecoin issuer's research arm (QVAC), published BotPsy on the Hugging Face blog: an on-device personal assistant built on a 0.8-billion-parameter agentic language model. alsoToday.headline: AI agents found a Maya site in lidar data, then learned it was known
alsoToday.summary: Pietro Miotti describes how his AI agents analysed NASA lidar data and flagged a Maya site in Mexico that was not in the register of the national heritage institute (INAH), going from a passing idea to an official government reply in under 72 hours.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: An idea worth copying: agents that sift public sensor data for anomalies, then check them against registers. The miss is the lesson, too: the literature check is the weak step.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: AI doing science and maths · day 5
alsoToday.detailHtml: Pietro Miotti describes how his AI agents analysed NASA lidar data and flagged a Maya site in Mexico that was not in the register of the national heritage institute (INAH), going from a passing idea to an official government reply in under 72 hours. An update on 11 November says archaeologists had in fact mapped it in a 2025 paper; the agents missed it while reviewing the literature. The post topped Hacker News with 917 points.

alsoToday.headline: Andreeva wins 11 straight games to rout Sabalenka at WTA Finals
alsoToday.summary: Mirra Andreeva, the 19-year-old French Open champion, came from 4-1 down to win 11 games in a row and beat world number two Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 6-0, reaching the last four at the WTA Finals, BBC Sport reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Andreeva joins Linda Noskova in the semi-finals.

alsoToday.headline: Tim Peters, author of the Zen of Python and Timsort, dies
alsoToday.summary: The Python community announced the death of Tim Peters (1952-2026) in an 'In Memoriam' post on discuss.python.org. Peters, a long-time Python core developer, wrote 'The Zen of Python' and created Timsort, the sorting algorithm later adopted by Java, Android and other platforms.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Timsort runs inside much of the world's software, including bank systems on the JVM.

alsoToday.headline: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner swap deal but no territory deal
alsoToday.summary: Russian and Ukrainian negotiators agreed in principle to a major prisoner exchange at two days of talks in Abu Dhabi that ended on Wednesday, their first negotiations in nine months, Reuters reports (via The Japan Times); numbers are still to be set.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A humanitarian step, not a ceasefire; European defence and reconstruction plans stay on their current track.
alsoToday.update: Talks ended Wednesday with a prisoner exchange agreed in principle; US says trust and territory still block a deal
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: talks to end the Ukraine war · day 3
alsoToday.detailHtml: Russian and Ukrainian negotiators agreed in principle to a major prisoner exchange at two days of talks in Abu Dhabi that ended on Wednesday, their first negotiations in nine months, Reuters reports (via The Japan Times); numbers are still to be set. US mediators, including Jared Kushner, said differences remain on major issues, including territory, and that a lack of trust is holding talks back.
